case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an insurer whose legally protected interests are not directly affected by confirmation of a Chapter 11 plan is nonetheless a statutory “party in interest” entitled under 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) to object and be heard on any issue in the case (including plan confirmation).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) (who may “raise and may appear and be heard on any issue” as a “party in interest” in Chapter 11); related standing doctrines as applied in bankruptcy plan-confirmation litigation.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Truck Insurance Exchange argues that § 1109(b) does not grant an unlimited right for insurers (or other outsiders) to litigate in Chapter 11 when the plan does not alter their legal rights or impose obligations on them. In Truck’s view, “party in interest” should be limited to entities with a concrete, legally protected stake that could be affected by the plan’s confirmation (e.g., by changing coverage obligations, impairing contractual rights, or binding the insurer via releases/injunctions). Allowing objections by parties whose rights are untouched invites strategic holdouts, drives up administrative and litigation costs, slows confirmation, and undermines Congress’s design for efficient reorganization—especially in complex mass-tort bankruptcies. Truck also aligns with the United States’ position that § 1109(b) is not an across-the-board authorization to participate absent a cognizable stake and should be read consistently with generally applicable standing principles and bankruptcy’s specialized limits on who may object to confirmation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The asbestos claimants’ committee and future claimants’ representative contend that § 1109(b) is deliberately broad and is meant to allow meaningful participation by those with practical and financial exposure in the reorganization, including insurers whose economic interests may be affected by how the plan structures claims resolution—even if the plan does not formally rewrite the insurance contract. Respondents argue that insurers often play a central role in funding and designing asbestos trusts and channeling injunction structures; insulating confirmation from insurer input would reduce transparency, increase the risk of collusive or imprudent plan terms, and impair the bankruptcy court’s ability to test feasibility and fairness. They also emphasize that Chapter 11 is a collective proceeding where plan terms can materially influence the insurer’s real-world exposure (e.g., through claim-processing rules, assignment/indemnity dynamics, and settlement leverage), and thus insurers should qualify as parties in interest entitled to be heard. Several respondent-side amici (bankruptcy experts and policyholder advocates) likewise stress that narrowing § 1109(b) would destabilize long-settled Chapter 11 practice and reduce participation that can improve the accuracy and integrity of plan confirmation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch are right that § 1109(b) is drafted broadly (“including,” “any issue”), but that breadth presupposes the antecedent limitation Congress chose: only a “party in interest” may invoke it, and we must give that phrase independent work. Justice Sotomayor’s practical-exposure and collusion concern is powerful as a policy matter, yet as a statutory rule it collapses the threshold into ubiquitous ripple-effects participation and effectively makes case-management, rather than text, do the limiting—an approach that sits uneasily with our institutional role. Justice Alito’s invocation of Hartford Underwriters strengthens the structural caution: we should not treat § 1109(b)’s general right to be heard as an engine for participation untethered to legal effects of confirmation, even if it is not a cause-of-action case. A narrow holding—insurers are parties in interest when confirmation can bind or alter their legal position (releases, injunctions, coverage-determinative provisions), but not when a plan is genuinely insurance-neutral—best respects text, bankruptcy tradition, and administrability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that § 1109(b) is textually expansive (“including,” “any issue”), but that breadth answers only what a qualifying entity may do, not who qualifies; the statute’s threshold—“party in interest”—must have limiting content or it becomes surplusage. Justice Sotomayor’s “practical exposure” test cannot be reconciled with the term’s original public meaning in bankruptcy practice, where participation at merits stages presupposed a legally cognizable stake in the estate or in rights the court can bind; otherwise ubiquitous downstream economic effects would convert § 1109(b) into a roving supervisory license. Hartford Underwriters, as Justice Alito notes, underscores the structural caution against reading general participatory language to expand bankruptcy litigation rights beyond those tied to legally affected interests, even if it does not control this precise question. I therefore remain persuaded by the Chief Justice’s and my own view: insurers are parties in interest when the plan legally alters or binds their position (releases, injunctions, coverage-determinative provisions), but not when it is genuinely insurance-neutral and leaves their contracts untouched.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1109(b) says a party in interest may be heard on “any issue” and uses “including,” which sounds intentionally expansive. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, that breadth is conditional on satisfying the threshold term Congress chose—“party in interest”—and a textualist reading must give that phrase limiting content tied to legally cognizable interests affected by confirmation, not ubiquitous downstream economic exposure. Justice Sotomayor’s practical-exposure/collusion concern is serious, yet it proves too much as a statutory test and would effectively convert confirmation into collateral coverage litigation whenever a plan reshapes incentives, inviting delay in a way Hartford Underwriters cautions against when general participatory language is used to circumvent the Code’s structural limits. I would recognize insurer participation where the plan binds or alters the insurer’s legal position (releases, injunctions, coverage-determinative mechanisms), but not where the plan genuinely leaves contractual rights untouched.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that “party in interest” must do real limiting work to prevent § 1109(b) from becoming an all-comers delay mechanism, and I share the concern about strategic obstruction. But their proposed limiter—requiring that confirmation legally alter the insurer’s rights—reads like an atextual “insurance-neutral” carve-out that conflicts with Congress’s deliberately expansive phrasing (“including” and “may … be heard on any issue”), especially at the trial-court stage where transparency is critical in mass-tort cases. Justice Alito’s reliance on Hartford Underwriters does not move me because that case addressed using § 1109(b) to create a cause of action reserved to a different actor under a different provision; recognizing an insurer’s right to be heard on feasibility, collusion, or plan architecture that predictably drives exposure does not transfer enforcement authority or circumvent any specific Code command. Workability is better protected through relevance limits and case-management at confirmation, with the stricter “person aggrieved” doctrine (which the Chief Justice invokes) doing the limiting work on appeal, rather than narrowing who gets heard when vulnerable claimants most need an adversarial test of the plan.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1109(b) promises a party in interest may be heard on “any issue,” and “including” signals an expansive, nonexclusive category. But that argument still depends on what counts as a “party in interest,” and I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas that this threshold term—read against Chapter 11’s stake-based structure—cannot be satisfied by ubiquitous downstream economic effects without making the limiter effectively vanish. Justice Sotomayor is right that case-management and transparency matter in mass-tort plans, yet her approach risks converting § 1109(b) into a general oversight license where the plan leaves the insurer’s legal rights untouched; that is precisely the kind of structural expansion Hartford Underwriters (as Justice Alito notes) counsels us to resist. Under a pragmatic textualism, the workable middle is to treat insurers as parties in interest when confirmation legally binds or alters their position (releases, injunctions, or coverage-determinative mechanisms), not when they allege only practical exposure from plan design.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas most forcefully argue that “party in interest” is the statutory limiter and should be read, in light of bankruptcy tradition, to require a legally affected stake rather than mere economic exposure, especially where a plan is “insurance neutral.” But on the enacted text, § 1109(b)’s undefined “party in interest,” coupled with the expansive guarantee that such a party “may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” suggests Congress chose breadth at the trial level and did not codify a rights-alteration prerequisite for being heard at confirmation. Justice Alito’s reliance on Hartford Underwriters does not undermine that conclusion because Hartford rejected using § 1109(b) to create a cause of action under a different, actor-specific provision; allowing an insurer to be heard at confirmation does not transfer enforcement authority or displace any more specific Code command. Workability concerns Roberts raises are real, but they are better addressed by ordinary relevance and case-management limits (and the separate “person aggrieved” constraint on appellate standing) than by judicially narrowing “party in interest” to exclude entities with concrete, non-speculative exposure created by the plan’s structure.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that § 1109(b) says a party in interest may be heard on “any issue” and uses an “including” list, which on its face is expansive and resists judicial carve-outs. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, that breadth is triggered only after crossing Congress’s threshold—“party in interest”—and reading that term to include anyone with downstream economic exposure would effectively erase the limiter and invite the strategic delay and loss of Chapter 11 workability the Chief identifies. Justice Sotomayor is right that mass-tort plan architecture can predictably shift real-world exposure, yet Hartford Underwriters cautions against converting general participation language into a roving supervisory license untethered to legally cognizable interests; case-management cannot replace the statutory boundary. I would therefore keep the line at whether confirmation legally affects or binds the insurer (releases, injunctions, coverage-determining provisions), not merely whether the plan may increase claims and thus costs in practice.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that “party in interest” must limit § 1109(b) to prevent strategic delay, but their proposed limiter—requiring that confirmation itself legally alter or bind the insurer’s rights—adds atextual conditions onto Congress’s broad command that a party in interest “may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” with “including” signaling an expansive, nonexclusive category. Justice Thomas’s term-of-art framing is not decisive here because the Code leaves “party in interest” undefined, and in Chapter 11 Congress plausibly chose broad trial-level participation while relying on ordinary relevance/case-management tools, Article III constraints, and (as the Chief Justice notes) the distinct appellate “person aggrieved” doctrine to prevent overbreadth. Justice Alito’s Hartford Underwriters concern is real, but it addresses using § 1109(b) to seize actor-specific causes of action; allowing an insurer with a concrete financial stake to be heard at confirmation does not confer enforcement power or rewrite any more specific Code provision. If the plan is truly insurance-neutral, bankruptcy courts can deny discovery or limit objections on relevance and burden grounds, but that is different from redefining “party in interest” to exclude materially affected stakeholders at the threshold.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest textual push: § 1109(b) says a party in interest may be heard on “any issue,” and “including” signals breadth. But that breadth presupposes the threshold term Congress chose—“party in interest”—and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas that reading it to cover anyone with downstream economic exposure collapses the limiter in a way that is especially problematic in Chapter 11, where ripple effects are ubiquitous and delay itself can be coercive. Justice Sotomayor’s collusion/transparency concern is real in mass-tort plans, yet under my pragmatic, procedural-fairness lens it is better addressed by robust disclosure and targeted discovery once a legally cognizable stake is shown, rather than by turning § 1109(b) into an all-comers objection right. Hartford Underwriters, as Justice Alito emphasizes, strengthens my hesitation to treat § 1109(b)’s general “be heard” language as a roving license untethered to legal effects; the more workable, fair line is whether confirmation itself alters or binds the insurer’s legal position (releases, injunctions, coverage-determining provisions), not merely whether it changes incentives in ways that might increase payouts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1109(b) must be read in light of bankruptcy’s long-settled limits on who may litigate particular issues, including the “person aggrieved” requirement for appellate review, which reflects a consistent insistence that participation track a concrete, legally cognizable stake rather than generalized policy objections. Where a plan is “insurance neutral” and does not alter an insurer’s contractual obligations or otherwise bind it through releases or injunctions, treating the insurer as a statutory “party in interest” entitled to object to confirmation would expand participation beyond those whose legally protected interests are affected, inviting delay and undermining efficient reorganization—an outcome Congress is unlikely to have intended from the phrase “party in interest” in § 1109(b). A narrow holding preserves institutional legitimacy by allowing insurer participation when plan terms actually affect insurer rights, while preventing objection rights from becoming a freestanding vehicle to influence plan design absent direct legal impact. This approach respects federalism and the Bankruptcy Code’s structure by keeping bankruptcy adjudication tied to concrete effects rather than abstract oversight.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1109(b) allows a “party in interest” to “raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” but the text does not define that term to include entities whose legally protected rights are untouched by confirmation, and an original public-meaning reading treats “party in interest” as a term of art tied to a concrete stake. Under the interpretive principle that transplanted legal terms bring their established meaning with them, see Taggart v. Lorenzen, 139 S. Ct. 1795, 1801 (2019), Congress’s use of “party in interest” in 1978 should be read against prior usage where it was effectively coextensive with standing-like limits, not as an unlimited license for outsiders to litigate. Reading § 1109(b) to confer participation rights absent any cognizable, legally affected interest would also collide with the baseline requirement that federal courts adjudicate concrete disputes rather than generalized objections, a limit statutes do not lightly displace. Because an “insurance-neutral” plan that neither alters coverage obligations nor binds the insurer through releases or injunctions does not affect the insurer’s legally protected interests, the insurer is not a statutory “party in interest” entitled to object to confirmation under § 1109(b).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard,” but it does not plausibly confer an unlimited entitlement to litigate plan confirmation when the insurer’s legally protected interests are not affected; “party in interest” should be read to require a concrete stake consistent with bankruptcy standing principles. As Hartford Underwriters explains, § 1109(b)’s general participation language cannot be read so broadly as to override other, more specific limits in the Code or to create implied, freewheeling rights of participation untethered to an affected legal interest. A contrary reading invites strategic holdouts and increased administrative costs, undermining the practical, Congress-designed efficiency of Chapter 11 without clear textual warrant. Therefore, an insurer whose rights and obligations are untouched by confirmation is not a statutory “party in interest” entitled to object to confirmation under § 1109(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1109(b) provides that a “party in interest … may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” and that broad language is best read to include insurers with concrete economic exposure to how a Chapter 11 plan structures claims resolution, even if the plan does not formally rewrite the insurance contract. The Third Circuit’s approach in In re Global Industrial Technologies correctly treats § 1109(b) as a broad participation statute at the trial level—at least coextensive with Article III standing—so courts can hear objections alleging collusion or plan structures that practically shift liability and threaten fairness. Excluding insurers whose real-world exposure is affected would reduce transparency and undermine the bankruptcy court’s ability to test feasibility and integrity of mass-tort plans that most directly impact vulnerable claimants. Prudential limits can be managed through case-management and relevance rulings rather than a cramped reading of § 1109(b) that risks insulating problematic plans from meaningful scrutiny.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard on any issue” only to a “party in interest,” a term that—read in context with Chapter 11’s structure and Article III limits—presupposes some concrete stake that the plan’s confirmation can affect, not merely a generalized interest in how the case is run. Where a plan is genuinely “insurance neutral” and does not alter the insurer’s contractual obligations, impair its rights, or bind it through releases or injunctions, treating the insurer as a § 1109(b) objector would convert that provision into an open-ended license for outsiders to litigate any issue, undermining workability and the Bankruptcy Code’s goal of efficient reorganization. That narrower reading still leaves room for insurer participation when plan terms realistically change legal exposure (e.g., channeling injunctions, assignments, or coverage-determining provisions), and it aligns § 1109(b) with bankruptcy’s traditional “person aggrieved” limits on who may contest plan-related rulings. The contrary approach risks strategic holdouts and administrative delay in complex mass-tort Chapter 11 cases without a clear textual command to permit objections by parties whose legally protected interests are untouched.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1109(b) provides that a “party in interest … may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue” in a Chapter 11 case, and its text signals breadth rather than atextual carve-outs like an “insurance neutrality” limitation. While Article III still requires a concrete stake for federal-court adjudication, nothing in § 1109(b)’s words authorizes courts to impose additional, judge-made prudential barriers beyond those constitutional minima, especially where an insurer alleges a real financial exposure tied to plan structure even if the plan purports not to rewrite the policy. Reading “party in interest” to include those with a practical financial stake better accords with the statute’s ordinary meaning and with bankruptcy’s design as a collective proceeding in which plan terms can materially affect distributions and litigation posture. The contrary approach risks substituting policy balancing for the enacted text and invites courts to invent categorical exclusions untethered to § 1109(b)’s language.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1109(b) is a general participation provision, but it should be read in harmony with the Bankruptcy Code’s structure and longstanding limits that tie plan-confirmation objections to a concrete stake in the outcome, rather than granting open-ended participation to entities whose legally protected interests are unaffected. As Hartford Underwriters explains, we do not read § 1109(b)’s broad “right to be heard” to authorize actions or participation that other, more specific Code provisions implicitly cabin to affected parties, reinforcing a restrained, text-and-structure-based reading. Allowing an insurer to object to confirmation when the plan neither alters its contractual obligations nor binds it via releases/injunctions would undermine practical workability by inviting strategic delay and increasing administrative costs in complex reorganizations. Consistent with precedent, history, and institutional concerns, § 1109(b) should not be construed to expand participation beyond parties whose rights or obligations are meaningfully implicated by confirmation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) is deliberately expansive: a “party in interest … may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” and the statute’s illustrative list (“including”) signals breadth rather than limitation to only those whose rights are formally modified by a plan. Reading “party in interest” to exclude insurers whenever a plan is styled “insurance neutral” risks importing an atextual, judge-made limitation that Congress did not enact—especially given that Congress elsewhere used narrowing language like “person aggrieved” when it meant to restrict participation. Methodological consistency favors distinguishing the statutory right to be heard in the bankruptcy court from the more demanding “person aggrieved” limits often applied to bankruptcy appeals, thereby avoiding rewriting § 1109(b) while still leaving other doctrinal checks in place. Because an insurer can have a cognizable stake in the structure and administration of a mass-tort plan even absent formal alteration of the policy terms, it qualifies as a statutory “party in interest” entitled to object and be heard at confirmation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1109(b)’s broad language (“may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue”) cannot be read to erase the limiting principle that participation in federal court generally requires a concrete stake; otherwise, plan confirmation could be derailed by entities whose legally protected interests are not implicated, undermining Chapter 11’s practical function and fairness to parties whose rights are actually at issue. The best reconciliation is that an insurer qualifies as a “party in interest” only when the plan’s confirmation could affect a legally protected interest—consistent with In re James Wilson Assocs., 965 F.2d 160, 169 (7th Cir. 1992), and with bankruptcy’s traditional “person aggrieved” limits on who may object or seek review. That approach preserves meaningful insurer participation when plans alter coverage obligations or impose releases/injunctions, while preventing strategic or collateral objections that increase costs and delay without corresponding procedural-fairness benefits. This reading also aligns with the Ninth Circuit’s refusal to treat § 1109(b) as coextensive with Article III standing, see In re Tower Park Props., LLC, 803 F.3d 450, 457 & n.6 (9th Cir. 2015).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an insurer whose legally protected rights are not directly affected by confirmation of a Chapter 11 plan nonetheless qualifies as a “party in interest” under 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) and may therefore object and be heard on any issue in the case.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) (Chapter 11 “party in interest” right to appear and be heard); related standing concepts reflected in bankruptcy appellate “person aggrieved” doctrine and Article III standing principles (as framing concepts, not the direct statutory text at issue).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Truck Insurance Exchange argues that § 1109(b)’s “party in interest” is not an open-ended license for any economically or strategically interested entity to litigate in Chapter 11. Instead, participation should be limited to parties whose legally protected interests are actually affected by the plan or the proceeding; because Truck’s policy obligations and rights are not altered by the Kaiser Gypsum plan (i.e., the plan does not impair or determine Truck’s contractual coverage defenses/obligations), Truck is not a qualifying “party in interest” for purposes of objecting to plan confirmation. Allowing unaffected insurers to object would expand bankruptcy participation beyond the statute’s purpose, create delay and leverage-driven litigation, and disrupt the structure of Chapter 11 and asbestos reorganizations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The asbestos claimants’ committee and the future claimants’ representative argue that § 1109(b) is intentionally broad and grants a right to be heard to entities with a sufficient stake in the Chapter 11 case, not only those whose rights are formally modified by the plan. They contend an insurer can be a “party in interest” because plan structure, claim resolution mechanisms, and channeling/trust features can materially affect the insurer’s practical exposure, litigation posture, and indemnity/defense costs, even if the plan purports not to adjudicate coverage. They further argue bankruptcy courts historically permit robust participation by constituencies with a real financial interest to ensure fairness, transparency, and accurate information, and that narrowing § 1109(b) would impede effective administration—especially in mass-tort/asbestos cases where insurers are central economic actors.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual breadth—§ 1109(b)’s “including” (as § 102(3) confirms) and “on any issue” signal an expansive participatory right, and bankruptcy courts can manage abuse. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch argue, the phrase doing the limiting work is still “party in interest,” and reading that term to include any actor with downstream economic exposure would erase the statute’s threshold and convert § 1109(b) into a roving license untethered to the confirmation order’s legal effects, contrary to Hartford Underwriters’ structural caution against using general participation language to expand bankruptcy litigation beyond the Code’s allocations. Justice Thomas is right that Hartford involved a trustee-specific power, but its interpretive warning remains relevant here: we should not let a broad procedural grant swallow the Code’s rights-adjusting focus by treating leverage as a legally cognizable “interest.” The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is to hold only that where a plan is genuinely insurance-neutral—neither adjudicating nor impairing coverage rights—an insurer is not a party in interest to object to confirmation, while leaving open participation when the plan or confirmation order binds or alters the insurer’s legal position.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that “party in interest” must do limiting work and should not extend to anyone with downstream economic exposure, especially where a plan is styled “insurance-neutral.” But their proposed “legally cognizable interest/insurance-neutrality” gloss is not anchored in § 1109(b)’s text, which grants participatory rights to a “party in interest” to be heard “on any issue,” and Congress’s § 102(3) instruction that “including” is nonlimiting forecloses narrowing based on the listed exemplars alone. Hartford Underwriters, invoked by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan, does not undermine this reading because it concerned who may exercise a trustee-specific statutory power, not whether an affected entity may appear and be heard at confirmation under an express participatory grant. Whatever administrability concerns attend insurer objections, under an original public meaning approach we cannot add an atextual requirement that the confirmation order formally adjudicate or impair coverage rights before an insurer facing channeled, trust-processed claims may be heard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest textual point—§ 1109(b) says a party in interest may be heard “on any issue,” and § 102(3) makes “including” non-limiting—but that still leaves the antecedent question of what counts as an “interest” in this statutory setting. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the enumerated exemplars point to entities with a legally cognizable stake that the confirmation order itself will alter, bind, or adjudicate; reading “interest” to include any actor with downstream economic exposure drains the term of limiting force and turns § 1109(b) into a roving license for collateral leverage. Justice Thomas is right that Hartford Underwriters is not perfectly on point, but Justice Gorsuch properly invokes its structural caution against using general participatory language to expand bankruptcy litigation beyond the Code’s rights-adjusting framework—especially where the plan is genuinely insurance-neutral and expressly preserves all coverage defenses. The respondents’ reliance on case-management tools cannot substitute for a statutory threshold, and under a textualist, context-sensitive reading, contingent practical effects alone do not make an insurer a “party in interest” to object to confirmation in these circumstances.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that “party in interest” must do limiting work, and that an “insurance-neutral” plan ostensibly preserving defenses may mean the insurer lacks a legally cognizable stake in the confirmation order itself. But that limitation is not grounded in § 1109(b)’s text, which—paired with § 102(3)’s non-limiting “including” and the right to be heard “on any issue”—signals Congress chose openness at confirmation, leaving tailoring to bankruptcy judges rather than an insurer-specific carveout. Justice Gorsuch’s Hartford Underwriters analogy is not persuasive here because Hartford policed who may wield a trustee-assigned avoiding power, whereas this case concerns who may participate in a confirmation hearing—precisely the proceeding § 1109(b) addresses. And even so-called insurance-neutral mass-tort plans can practically reconfigure exposure through channeling, trust criteria, and releases, so a categorical exclusion risks insulating unfair or collusive structures from adversarial testing to the detriment of present and future claimants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best textual point: § 1109(b) is broad—“including” (via § 102(3)) and “on any issue” signal an expansive right to be heard, and mass-tort plan architecture can have serious practical consequences even when styled “insurance-neutral.” But that breadth still presupposes the threshold category “party in interest,” and I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that reading “interest” as any downstream economic exposure collapses the term’s limiting function and untethers participation from the legal rights the confirmation order actually adjusts. Hartford Underwriters, while not identical (as Justice Thomas notes), reinforces the structural caution against using § 1109(b)’s general participation language to expand bankruptcy litigation beyond Code-allocated, rights-adjusting stakes—especially where the plan expressly preserves coverage defenses and avoids binding the insurer. On a pragmatic textualist view, the best middle ground is a narrow holding: insurers may be parties in interest when the plan or confirmation order legally binds, impairs, or adjudicates their coverage/defense obligations, but not when the plan is genuinely insurance-neutral and leaves their legal position unchanged.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Jackson press the strongest point for Respondent: § 1109(b)’s “including” and “on any issue” are undeniably broad, and Hartford Underwriters involved a trustee-only power rather than confirmation participation. But that breadth operates only once an entity is a “party in interest,” and the statute does not define “interest” as any practical or downstream exposure; read in context with the listed exemplars, it denotes a legally cognizable stake that the confirmation order itself alters, adjudicates, or binds. Hartford Underwriters still matters as structural guidance, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, because it cautions against treating § 1109(b) as a roving warrant to expand bankruptcy litigation in ways that upset the Code’s allocations—here, by letting non-rights-holders litigate plan confirmation based on leverage alone. Amatex/Global Industrial (raised by Justice Jackson) shows some courts adopt a pragmatic approach, but those decisions are best read to allow insurer participation when a plan actually affects coverage/defense obligations; they do not defeat the textual-contextual point that a genuinely insurance-neutral plan leaves the insurer’s legal position untouched.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the best textual point: § 1109(b) is broad (“including,” per § 102(3), and “on any issue”), and in mass-tort cases plan architecture can practically affect insurers even if rights are nominally reserved. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the term “party in interest” still must do limiting work in context; otherwise “any issue” becomes a roving license for anyone with downstream economic exposure to litigate at confirmation, a reading in tension with the Code’s structured allocations and Hartford Underwriters’ caution against using § 1109(b) to expand participation beyond legally affected stakes. I am not persuaded that practical leverage, divorced from any adjudication or impairment of coverage rights in the confirmation order, suffices to create the requisite “interest” for a confirmation objection—especially where the plan is genuinely insurance-neutral and expressly preserves all insurer defenses. We should therefore hold narrowly for Petitioner on insurance-neutral plans, while leaving open insurer standing when a plan actually binds, impairs, or adjudicates coverage obligations or defenses.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best textual point: § 1109(b)’s “including” (as § 102(3) confirms) and “on any issue” are capacious, and insurers may feel substantial practical effects even under a plan styled “insurance-neutral.” But that breadth still presupposes the threshold category “party in interest,” and—consistent with the contextual exemplar list emphasized by the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan—the most natural reading limits that term to entities whose legally cognizable rights or distributional entitlements are altered, adjudicated, or bound in the confirmation process, not merely those with downstream economic leverage. Hartford Underwriters, while not on all fours (as Justice Thomas notes), reinforces the structural caution against converting § 1109(b) into a roving license to litigate collateral disputes absent a legally affected stake; case-management cannot substitute for that statutory boundary. I therefore remain persuaded that where the confirmation order genuinely preserves coverage defenses and does not bind or adjudicate insurer obligations, practical exposure alone does not confer “party in interest” status to object to confirmation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed “insurance-neutral plan” carveout and Justice Kagan’s concern that “party in interest” must do limiting work are the strongest opposing points, but they both effectively add a requirement that the confirmation order legally adjudicate or impair coverage rights—language Congress did not put in § 1109(b), especially given § 102(3)’s instruction that “including” is non-limiting and § 1109(b)’s grant to be heard “on any issue.” Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Hartford Underwriters does not move me because Hartford warned against using § 1109(b) to seize a discrete Code power assigned to “the trustee,” whereas participation at confirmation is exactly the kind of information-forcing, adversarial testing § 1109(b) affirmatively authorizes for parties with real stakes. Even when a plan labels itself insurance-neutral, mass-tort plan architecture (channeling injunctions, trust criteria, releases, claim-processing rules) can practically and predictably reshape exposure and bargaining positions, and excluding insurers categorically risks insulating structurally unfair or collusive arrangements from scrutiny—an outcome inconsistent with procedural fairness. Administrability and delay are genuine, but as Justice Sotomayor notes, bankruptcy courts have targeted tools to manage abusive participation without rewriting the statutory threshold.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to be heard to a “party in interest,” but that term should be read to require a concrete, legally cognizable stake in the confirmation dispute, not merely a strategic or economic concern untethered to alteration of the objector’s rights. Reading § 1109(b) as coextensive with Article III standing, as the Third Circuit suggested in In re Global Industrial Technologies, 645 F.3d 201 (3d Cir. 2011) (en banc), risks expanding participation in ways that invite delay and leverage-driven litigation, undermining the orderly administration of Chapter 11 and institutional legitimacy. A narrower construction—limiting insurer objections where the plan does not impair or adjudicate the insurer’s coverage rights—better aligns with bankruptcy’s traditional “person aggrieved” constraints on who may litigate plan confirmation issues and respects Congress’s structural choices in Chapter 11. Because Truck’s legally protected coverage defenses and obligations are not altered by the plan, it is not a “party in interest” entitled to object to confirmation under § 1109(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 11 U.S.C. § 1109(b) provides that a “party in interest, including” enumerated case stakeholders (e.g., creditor, equity security holder, indenture trustee) “may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue,” and the open-ended “including” signals a broad, non-exhaustive category rather than a closed list limited to those whose rights are formally altered by the plan. Read in its historical bankruptcy usage and ordinary meaning, “party in interest” refers to those with a legally cognizable stake in the reorganization (not mere bystanders), and an insurer facing practical exposure and costs tied to plan structure can fall within that class even if the plan purports to be “insurance neutral.” Nothing in § 1109(b)’s text conditions participation on the plan’s direct impairment of the objector’s contractual rights, and courts should not graft atextual prudential limits like an “insurance neutrality” carveout onto Congress’s broad grant to be heard “on any issue.” Any narrowing of that statutory entitlement is for Congress, not for courts applying extra-textual doctrines.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1109(b) lists exemplars—“the debtor, the trustee, a creditors’ committee, an equity security holders’ committee, a creditor, an equity security holder, or any indenture trustee”—all of which have legally protected interests in the case, and the phrase “party in interest” should be read in that context rather than as an open-ended invitation for any entity with a strategic or economic concern to litigate plan confirmation. Where a plan is “insurance neutral” and does not alter the insurer’s contractual rights or coverage defenses, the insurer is not the sort of affected stakeholder Congress contemplated as entitled to object to confirmation “on any issue” under § 1109(b). That narrower reading aligns with bankruptcy’s emphasis on efficient reorganization and with courts’ recognition that unimpaired stakeholders are deemed to accept the plan, see 11 U.S.C. §§ 1124, 1126(f), and avoids leverage-driven delay by parties whose rights are not being adjudicated. The Ninth Circuit’s approach rejecting the idea that § 1109(b) is coextensive with Article III standing better reflects the statutory structure than the Third Circuit’s expansive rule.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard on any issue,” and its non-exhaustive list (reinforced by 11 U.S.C. § 102(3)’s rule that “including” is “not limiting”) indicates Congress intended broad participation where an entity has a concrete stake in the case’s administration and outcomes. In mass-tort Chapter 11 cases, plan design and claims-resolution mechanisms can materially affect an insurer’s practical exposure, defense costs, and litigation posture even if the plan purports not to adjudicate coverage, so excluding insurers categorically would risk insulating potentially unfair or collusive structures from meaningful scrutiny. The Third Circuit’s approach in In re Global Industrial Technologies, Inc., 645 F.3d 201 (3d Cir. 2011), treating § 1109(b) as a broad participation provision (at least coextensive with Article III standing), better serves transparency and fairness—especially for vulnerable present and future claimants—than a cramped reading that limits objections only to formally impaired legal rights. Allowing a voice at confirmation advances accurate information-gathering and equitable administration without pre-judging the insurer’s ultimate contract defenses, which can still be litigated in the proper forum.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard” to a “party in interest,” but that phrase is best read—consistent with statutory coherence and workability—to require a legally cognizable stake that the plan or proceeding actually affects, not merely a strategic or economic interest in how the case is structured. Reading “party in interest” as open-ended would invite insurer-driven confirmation litigation even where the plan expressly leaves coverage rights untouched, undermining efficient Chapter 11 administration and turning confirmation into leverage rather than a forum for resolving affected rights. Hartford Underwriters cautions that § 1109(b)’s general participatory language cannot be read to override the Code’s more tailored allocations of who may invoke particular bankruptcy processes, reinforcing that § 1109(b) is not an all-purpose license to litigate any issue. Where, as here, the plan does not impair or adjudicate the insurer’s contractual defenses or obligations, the insurer falls outside the practical and textual core of § 1109(b)’s “party in interest” for purposes of objecting to confirmation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard” to a “party in interest,” but that term cannot be read as an open-ended invitation for any entity with a practical or strategic stake when the plan does not affect its legally protected rights. As Hartford Underwriters instructs, § 1109(b)’s general participatory language does not authorize participation that would effectively expand bankruptcy litigation beyond limits set by the Code’s structure and the particular issues properly in dispute. Reading “party in interest” to require an interest the plan or proceeding actually affects accords with the ordinary meaning of “interest,” respects separation-of-powers limits by not enlarging statutory participation by policy impulse, and avoids converting Chapter 11 into a forum for collateral disputes untethered to plan effects. Because Truck’s contractual coverage rights and obligations are not impaired or determined by confirmation, it is not a “party in interest” entitled to object to confirmation under § 1109(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to “appear and be heard,” but it does not create an open-ended entitlement for any entity with a practical or strategic interest to object to confirmation; the better reading, consistent with history and workable administration of Chapter 11, limits “party in interest” to those whose legally protected interests are actually affected in the case. As Hartford Underwriters instructs, we should not read § 1109(b)’s general participatory language to override or expand the Code’s more specific structural limits, and participation should not be allowed to become a vehicle for leverage and delay where the plan does not alter the insurer’s contractual rights or obligations. That narrower construction also accords with traditional bankruptcy standing principles (including the “person aggrieved” limitation on appeals) and respects judicial restraint by keeping objections tethered to concrete legal effects rather than broader policy disputes. Because Truck’s coverage defenses and contractual obligations are not determined or impaired by confirmation, it is not a “party in interest” entitled to object under § 1109(b) on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1109(b) grants a right to be heard to a “party in interest,” but the enumerated examples (“creditors,” “equity security holders,” “indenture trustee,” etc.) share a common attribute: each has a legally protected stake in the estate or the plan’s legal effects, so the residual phrase should be read in that company rather than as an open-ended invitation to any economically interested bystander. Reading “party in interest” to include an insurer whose contractual rights and obligations are not altered or adjudicated by plan confirmation (i.e., an “insurance-neutral” plan) would detach the term from its statutory context and allow participation untethered to legally cognizable effects, contrary to the Code’s structure and the traditional bankruptcy limitation to those aggrieved. Consistent with long-standing appellate limits in bankruptcy, the “person aggrieved” doctrine reflects the appropriate narrowing principle: participation (and especially objection to confirmation) should be reserved for those directly and adversely affected in a pecuniary or legal sense by the order. Because Truck’s coverage defenses and obligations remain intact and unadjudicated under the plan, it is not a “party in interest” under § 1109(b) for confirmation objections.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1109(b) provides that a “party in interest … may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue” in a Chapter 11 case, and its inclusive list signals breadth rather than a narrow, rights-modification-only test. Consistent with that text, courts have construed “party in interest” pragmatically to include entities with a sufficient stake that may be materially affected by the reorganization process, even when the plan purports not to adjudicate their ultimate rights—an approach particularly salient in asbestos cases where plan structure can shape an insurer’s practical exposure, costs, and litigation posture. In re Amatex Corp. instructs that § 1109(b) “must be construed broadly to permit parties affected by a chapter 11 proceeding to appear and be heard,” aligning with procedural fairness by ensuring the court receives relevant information from economically central actors. While participation can impose delay costs, bankruptcy courts retain case-management tools to prevent leverage-driven obstruction without rewriting § 1109(b) to exclude insurers categorically when they have a real stake in confirmation.
